column3: Contrasts the final-day security of God's servants with the denied aid announced to the focus's addressees.
The denial of return after death supplies a remote antecedent to the final judgment assumed by the focus.
Their claim that a united group will prevail contrasts with the focus's declaration that no help will arrive.
Its use of today concerns excluding the needy and does not clarify the final-day cry or denied help.
The immediate continuation identifies arrogant, hostile treatment of the recited signs behind the verdict of 23:65.
It states that wrongdoing leaves a person without help from God, though in a different prophetic dispute.
It places wrongdoers in shared punishment on the day when benefit is impossible, closely framing futile appeal.
The immediate predecessor records their cry when punishment seizes them, which 23:65 directly forbids as useless.
Lawful self-defense after oppression is only a broad contrast to the failed aid of the final judgment.
It directly commands the condemned not to cry out today, intensifying the focus's rejection of their appeal.
The revival of dead land and ensuing emergence supplies a resurrection horizon for the decisive day in the focus.
People cry to God when hardship strikes, providing the temporal contrast to the focus's point when crying no longer avails.
Reliance on wrongdoers ends in the Fire with neither protectors nor help from God.
The nearby diagnosis of heedless hearts and persistent deeds supplies the moral background to 23:65.
Those in the Fire can only ask for one day of relief, showing how desperate appeal has become severely limited.
It calls for return before punishment comes, after which there will be no help, matching the focus's closed threshold.
The believing group's fear of returning to its Lord is a local contrast to the heedlessness and later cry of the focus's addressees.
On that day excuses are barred because recompense follows deeds, closely explaining why the focus rejects their plea.
Resurrection on the Day of Rising establishes the eschatological setting in which the focus says today.
At the exposure of secrets, neither personal strength nor any helper remains, directly paralleling denied aid.
God's powerful help to the messenger is a general positive contrast but adds little to the final judgment setting.
The condemned are addressed today, confined to the Fire, and told that they have no helpers.
The nearby true-speaking record and absence of injustice ground the fairness of the verdict in 23:65.
The same surah's final-day recompense of the patient provides a positive counterpart to the focus's exclusion.
The statement that the visitors are unfamiliar does not illuminate crying out or final-day help.
Support of God and His messenger by the emigrants is a distant positive use of help.
The final-day challenge, "Why do you not help one another?", exposes the collapse of mutual assistance.
Death is part of the local surah's earlier resurrection sequence but does not add to the focus's immediate warning.
The immediate continuation states that God's signs were recited but they turned back, specifying the rejected response.
God as guide and helper to each prophet is only a broad positive contrast to the focus's denied aid.
The announcement of painful punishment supports the consequence assumed by the adjacent failed-help scene.
Rules for distributing gains do not clarify the focus's eschatological cry or denied help.
God as the excellent protector and helper gives only a general positive contrast.
Alleged gods cannot help even themselves and cannot be protected from God, directly undermining hoped-for rescue.
The command to leave them in heedlessness until a time anticipates the local reversal expressed in 23:65.
The judged people's distorted sense of time develops the final-day setting within the same surah.
Temporary mercy and enjoyment until an appointed time only broadly precede the final outcome.
The returning sky image does not itself clarify the final-day refusal of help.
Wrongdoers have neither protector nor helper, a useful but general formulation of the focus's consequence.
Conflicting speech does not materially develop the focus's cry, day, or denied aid.
Their mistaken reading of wealth and children as good helps explain the local complacency before punishment.
A prophet's plea for help against corrupters is a distant positive counterpart to the help refused in the focus.
Calling on God in distress then forgetting Him offers a broad behavioral parallel to the later futile cry.
The command to abandon defilement does not clarify the focus.
Divine aid in a historical conflict is not the final-day withdrawal of aid at issue here.
The promised absence of fear and grief for sincere givers gives only a broad positive final-outcome contrast.
The nearby believers' fear of their Lord supplies a local contrast to the heedlessness punished in 23:65.
Promised divine help and near victory are a general positive contrast rather than an explanation of final refusal.
God's ability to defeat opponents while testing people is only indirectly related to the focus's denied rescue.
The trumpet blast initiates the difficult day that gives the focus's "today" its eschatological force.
God's dominion over life and death is joined to the absence of any protector or helper apart from Him.
Today every soul is repaid without injustice, directly supplying the judicial logic of the focus's final verdict.
Belief in the Lord's signs is a nearby positive contrast to the turning away stated after the focus.
A messenger's appeal for help after being called a liar reinforces the same-surah pattern before the final punishment scene.
On the appointed day neither schemes nor external help benefit the condemned, closely matching 23:65.
Human creation from gushing fluid does not add to this focus's cry or withdrawal of help.
Those cursed by God find no helper, a general consequence parallel without the final-day setting.
The command to separate today, addressed to criminals, gives a close final-day counterpart to the focus's address.
Rejecting association with the Lord is a nearby positive trait that contrasts with the focus's condemned group.
Help comes only from God and reassures believers, but it remains a broad positive formulation.
On the day when no close relation can avail another, none of them will be helped.
The collapse of confidence in fortified defenses offers only a worldly precursor to the focus's failed rescue.
The assurance that messengers are helped is a general positive contrast with limited marginal value.
The oath by the promised day reinforces the appointed final horizon presupposed by "today."
The local correction of their assumption about worldly goods continues the buildup to their punishment and cry.
It challenges the illusion that an army can help apart from the Merciful, directly questioning alternative rescue.
The warning about the Day of Calling gives a named final-day horizon for the focus's address.
Mutual generosity among believers does not clarify the condemned cry or the denial of aid.
No one can escape God and none has a protector or helper apart from Him.
Its question about the deferred day provides only a minimal temporal parallel.
The command to purify clothing does not illuminate the focus.
The general absence of a protector or helper apart from God repeats a point already made more closely above.
The promise of respite and firm planning does not itself explain the final-day cry.
Wrongdoers having no helpers supplies a general moral consequence but lacks the focus's final-day scene.
The condemned are submissive today, clarifying the helpless posture behind the focus's rejected outcry.
God's help for one wronged after measured response is a distant positive contrast.
The statement of respite and firm planning does not add to the focus's specific warning.
Those led astray by desire have no helpers, a broad parallel already represented by clearer cards.
The oath by what is unseen does not clarify the focus.
On the feared day, no soul can compensate, intercede, ransom, or receive help for another.
It repeats the same no-compensation and no-help final-day formula after the stronger 2:48 card.
The legitimacy of measured self-redress after wrong is only a remote contrast to unavailable final aid.
Today each soul receives what it earned with no injustice, directly explaining the irreversible judgment of 23:65.
God's complete dominion and the absence of protector or helper are relevant but redundant with clearer formulations.
A human declaration of no blame today and forgiveness is a limited contrast to the divine final judgment.
God's power to aid those wronged is a historical positive contrast, not the focus's final denial.
Later punishment after a period of enjoyment offers only a broad outcome parallel.
Believers ask when God's help will come during trial, contrasting with the final point when help is no longer available.
Leaders calling to the Fire will not be helped on the Day of Rising, closely joining judgment and denied aid.
The arrival of God's help and victory is a broad positive use of help with little final-day relevance.
The reassurance not to fear at a birth announcement does not bear on the focus.
Those without divine guidance have no protectors who can help them apart from God.
The command to fear God and know that all will be gathered to Him supplies a final-accountability horizon.
Mutual aid among believers is a positive communal use of help, distant from its final withdrawal.
Belief in the Day of Recompense gives the moral horizon whose denial is enacted in the focus.
Its political restriction on taking protectors or helpers is not the final-day helplessness at issue.
Household etiquette and privacy rules do not clarify the focus.
Mutual protection and treaty-limited aid are historical community rules, not the focus's final verdict.
Calling one's council anticipates an ineffective human backing, but the verse alone remains indirect.
The supposed intermediary gods fail to help their worshippers when needed, directly exposing false sources of rescue.
At the gathering before God, those warned have no protector or intercessor apart from Him.
Those invoked apart from God cannot help their callers or even help themselves.
The claimed intercessors apart from God expose the false basis for expecting rescue.
On the day of exposure, followers and leaders alike admit that neither party can help the other against God.
Satan explicitly disowns any power to answer or rescue those who followed him.
When harm strikes at sea, all supposed helpers vanish and people call on God alone.
Neither a supporting group apart from God nor self-defense can rescue the ruined possessor.
The disbelievers will be unable to ward off the Fire from themselves and will not be helped.
At the trumpet blast, lineage and mutual inquiry cease, establishing the collapse of ordinary human support.
The condemned confess that misery overcame them and that they were astray, supplying the content of their helpless appeal.
Their plea to be taken out of the Fire is a direct later counterpart to the focus's rejected cry.
The command to remain abased and speak no more makes explicit the final termination of condemned appeals.
When people are told to call their alleged partners, the partners do not answer them.
On the Hour, the criminals despair, giving the emotional outcome of the focus's futile cry.
Their alleged partners provide no intercession, so they disavow the very associations once trusted.
Those called apart from God neither hear nor answer, and on the Day of Rising they deny the association.
Idols are taken in hope of help, directly naming the misplaced expectation reversed by the focus.
Those gods cannot help their worshippers, despite the worshippers' readiness to serve them.
All intercession belongs to God alone, setting the boundary for any hope of rescue.
The keepers of Hell reject the condemned people's request for relief as an unanswered call of disbelievers.
The false objects of invocation vanish, and the condemned know there is no escape.
Before the irreversible day, there will be neither refuge nor any way to deny its reality.
Those invoked apart from God possess no power of intercession except by divinely grounded testimony.
The Fire awaits them, and neither their acquisitions nor their protectors apart from God avail them.
On that day no ransom is accepted from disbelievers, closing another imagined route of rescue.
The condemned person has neither a devoted friend nor any sustaining relief in the final punishment.
On the Day of Judgment no close friend asks after another, underscoring the dissolution of human support.
No intercession benefits the condemned, directly excluding a central form of hoped-for aid.
The declaration that there is no refuge gives a concise final-day equivalent of the focus's denied help.
Before the Lord, none possess power to address Him without permission, limiting any appeal or mediation.
On the day when no soul can do anything for another, all command belongs to God alone.
